title: Treatment options for phimosis
intro: Phimosis is a tight foreskin that cannot be pulled back over the head of the penis. When it causes problems, treatment options range from steroid cream to surgery. In young boys, a tight foreskin is normal and usually does not need treatment. The choice depends on age, symptoms and personal preference.

sections.heading: When treatment is needed
paragraphs: Treatment is considered if the foreskin is scarred, causes pain, recurring infections of the foreskin and head, difficulty urinating, painful erections or hygiene problems. In boys, treatment is generally not needed before about five or six years unless there are complications such as repeated infection, since many loosen with growth.

sections.heading: Steroid cream and stretching
paragraphs: A steroid cream applied thinly to the tight area once or twice daily for four to eight weeks, with gentle stretching, loosens the foreskin in most cases. It is the preferred first treatment, avoiding surgery in many people. Side effects are minor, such as mild skin irritation. Success is greater in children and in non-scarred foreskin. The foreskin should not be forced back.

sections.heading: Surgical options
paragraphs: Circumcision, removal of all or part of the foreskin, is the standard operation if creams fail or there is scarring or recurring infection. It is usually done under general anaesthetic in children and local or general in adults, as day surgery, with recovery in one to two weeks. Alternatives include a preputioplasty, which widens the opening but keeps the foreskin, and adhesion release. Risks include bleeding, infection, changes in sensitivity and an unsatisfactory result.

sections.heading: Emergency situations
paragraphs: Paraphimosis is when a retracted foreskin becomes stuck behind the head of the penis and swells, which is painful and needs urgent medical attention, so do not wait. After treatment, the doctor may recommend circumcision to prevent recurrence.

sections.heading: Choosing the right option
paragraphs: Discuss with the doctor the likelihood of success, the recovery time, the risks and the effects of each option. For boys, involve the child in an age-appropriate way. Cultural, religious and personal views may matter. Ask for a second opinion if you feel unsure.

examples.title: Starting cream treatment
examples.text: Imagine your doctor recommends a steroid cream for your son. You could apply it as instructed, avoid forcing the skin and arrange a review after several weeks.

examples.title: Preparing for surgery
examples.text: Suppose circumcision is planned. You might ask about anaesthesia, wound care, when your child can return to school and which signs should prompt a call.
